claim: FOXC1 loss contributes to Dandy-Walker malformation (DWM), a common human cerebellar malformation.
source: FOXC1 loss contributes to Dandy-Walker malformation (DWM), a common human cerebellar malformation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact, supported by prior research.

claim: Complete Foxc1 loss leads to aberrations in proliferation, neuronal differentiation and migration in the embryonic mouse cerebellum.
source: Previously, we found that complete Foxc1 loss leads to aberrations in proliferation, neuronal differentiation and migration in the embryonic mouse cerebellum (Haldipur et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Haldipur et al., 2014).

claim: Hypomorphic Foxc1 mutant mice have granule and Purkinje cell abnormalities causing subsequent disruptions in postnatal cerebellar foliation and lamination.
source: We now demonstrate that hypomorphic Foxc1 mutant mice have granule and Purkinje cell abnormalities causing subsequent disruptions in postnatal cerebellar foliation and lamination.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hypomorphic Foxc1 mutant mice have a partially formed posterior lobule which echoes the posterior vermis DW 'tail sign' observed in human imaging studies.
source: Particularly striking is the presence of a partially formed posterior lobule which echoes the posterior vermis DW 'tail sign' observed in human imaging studies.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Aberrant migration of granule cell progenitors destined to form the posterior-most lobule causes the partially formed posterior lobule phenotype in Foxc1 mutant mice.
source: Lineage tracing experiments in Foxc1 mutant mouse cerebella indicate that aberrant migration of granule cell progenitors destined to form the posterior-most lobule causes this unique phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments presented in the manuscript (Figure 2).

claim: Rare human del chr 6p25 fetal cerebella demonstrate extensive phenotypic overlap with Foxc1 mutant mouse models.
source: Analyses of rare human del chr 6p25 fetal cerebella demonstrate extensive phenotypic overlap with our Foxc1 mutant mouse models, validating our DWM models and demonstrating that many key mechanisms controlling cerebellar development are likely conserved between mouse and human.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analyses of human and mouse tissue presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Many key mechanisms controlling cerebellar development are likely conserved between mouse and human.
source: Analyses of rare human del chr 6p25 fetal cerebella demonstrate extensive phenotypic overlap with our Foxc1 mutant mouse models, validating our DWM models and demonstrating that many key mechanisms controlling cerebellar development are likely conserved between mouse and human.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic overlap between mouse and human del chr 6p25 cases.

claim: Rare heterozygous deletions of the FOXC1 gene on human chromosome 6p25 are associated with DWM.
source: We previously reported that rare heterozygous deletions (del) of the forkhead box C1 (FOXC1) gene on human chromosome (chr) 6p25 are associated with DWM (2).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Both zones of neurogenesis, the ventricular zone and rhombic lip, are disrupted in Foxc1-/- mice.
source: We have also conducted an extensive phenotypic analysis of the Foxc1 homozygous null (Foxc1-/-) mice where we have shown that both zones of neurogenesis, the ventricular zone and rhombic lip, are disrupted in Foxc1-/- mice (Aldinger et al., 2009; Haldipur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Aldinger et al., 2009; Haldipur et al., 2014).

claim: Foxc1hith/hith mice are viable as adults.
source: These mice are viable as adults and display a unique posterior foliation defect that is strikingly similar to the DWM 'tail sign' which has been recently proposed to represent a pathognomonic feature of DWM (Bernardo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: The DWM 'tail sign' has been recently proposed to represent a pathognomonic feature of DWM.
source: These mice are viable as adults and display a unique posterior foliation defect that is strikingly similar to the DWM 'tail sign' which has been recently proposed to represent a pathognomonic feature of DWM (Bernardo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bernardo et al., 2015.

claim: Premature and abnormal migration of posterior vermis-fated rhombic lip derived cells causes the posterior foliation defect in Foxc1hith/hith mice.
source: We present mouse genetic lineage mapping data that identifies premature and abnormal migration of posterior vermis-fated rhombic lip (RL) derived cells as the cause for this striking phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by lineage mapping data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Three rare human fetal del chr 6p25 DWM cases show ectopic granule cell progenitors and Purkinje cells.
source: We also present the analyses of 3 rare human fetal del chr 6p25 DWM cases which show extensive phenotypic overlap with Foxc1 mutant mouse cerebellar defects, including ectopic granule cell progenitors (GCPs) and Purkinje cells, dysmorphic Bergmann glial fibers, and posterior vermis disorganization.
evidence: This is supported by analyses of human fetal tissue presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Three rare human fetal del chr 6p25 DWM cases show dysmorphic Bergmann glial fibers.
source: We also present the analyses of 3 rare human fetal del chr 6p25 DWM cases which show extensive phenotypic overlap with Foxc1 mutant mouse cerebellar defects, including ectopic granule cell progenitors (GCPs) and Purkinje cells, dysmorphic Bergmann glial fibers, and posterior vermis disorganization.
evidence: This is supported by analyses of human fetal tissue presented in Figure 4.

claim: Three rare human fetal del chr 6p25 DWM cases show posterior vermis disorganization.
source: We also present the analyses of 3 rare human fetal del chr 6p25 DWM cases which show extensive phenotypic overlap with Foxc1 mutant mouse cerebellar defects, including ectopic granule cell progenitors (GCPs) and Purkinje cells, dysmorphic Bergmann glial fibers, and posterior vermis disorganization.
evidence: This is supported by analyses of human fetal tissue presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Foxc1 mutant mice are validated as models for human DWM.
source: Since Foxc1 mutations in mice recapitulate multiple aspects of the developing and mature human del chr 6p25 DWM cerebellar pathology, these data validate Foxc1 mutant mice as models for human DWM.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic overlap between mouse and human cases.

claim: Competent meningeal signaling is required for multiple aspects of prenatal and postnatal cerebellar development.
source: Further, our analyses clearly demonstrate that competent meningeal signaling is required for multiple aspects of prenatal and postnatal cerebellar development.
evidence: This is inferred from the data presented in the manuscript showing disruptions in cerebellar development in Foxc1 mutants.

claim: One hallmark of human DWM is posterior vermis hypoplasia.
source: One hallmark of human DWM is posterior vermis hypoplasia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about DWM.

claim: The normal human cerebellar vermis has a trilobar appearance, with primary and secondary fissures readily distinguishable.
source: As illustrated in Figure 1A–B, the normal human cerebellar vermis has a trilobar appearance, with primary and secondary fissures readily distinguishable (Figure 1B, white arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1A-B showing normal human cerebellar anatomy.

claim: In normal human cerebellum, the posterior vermis lobules, below the secondary fissure, are well formed and a distinct choroid plexus is evident.
source: The posterior vermis lobules, below the secondary fissure, are well formed and a distinct choroid plexus is evident (Figure 1B, yellow arrowhead).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1B showing normal human cerebellar anatomy.

claim: The cerebellar vermis in del chr 6p25 DWM patients ranges from very hypoplastic and dysplastic to less severely affected.
source: In contrast, the cerebellar vermis in our del chr 6p25 DWM patient cohort (Aldinger et al., 2009) ranges from very hypoplastic and dysplastic (Figure 1C,D), to less severely affected (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1C-F showing variable severity in del chr 6p25 DWM patients.

claim: Individuals with del chr 6p25 share a common extended and dysplastic posterior vermis with an indistinct choroid plexus.
source: Regardless of the extent of dysplasia, these individuals with del chr 6p25 share a common extended and dysplastic posterior vermis with an indistinct choroid plexus.
evidence: This is supported by observations from Figure 1C-F.

claim: The DWM 'tail sign' may be pathognomonic for DWM.
source: This feature has recently been designated the DWM 'tail sign' and may be pathognomonic for DWM (Figure 1D,F, red arrowhead) (Bernardo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bernardo et al., 2015 and shown in Figure 1D,F.

claim: Foxc1-/- mice have substantial cerebellar abnormalities as neonates.
source: Foxc1-/- mice have substantial cerebellar abnormalities as neonates (Aldinger et al., 2009; Haldipur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: During embryogenesis, Foxc1-/- mice have dramatic VZ proliferative deficits and GABAergic neuronal migration defects in addition to RL abnormalities.
source: During embryogenesis, Foxc1-/- mice have dramatic VZ proliferative deficits and GABAergic neuronal migration defects in addition to RL abnormalities (Aldinger et al., 2009; Haldipur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Neonatal lethality in Foxc1-/- mice precludes evaluation of cerebellar foliation, which is a postnatal process in mice.
source: Neonatal lethality precludes evaluation of cerebellar foliation, which is a postnatal process in mice.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the Foxc1-/- model.

claim: Mouse Foxc1-/- phenotypes are more severe than those seen in del chr 6p25 patients who retain one functional FOXC1 allele.
source: Furthermore, mouse Foxc1-/-phenotypes are more severe than those seen in del chr 6p25 patients who retain one functional FOXC1 allele.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing mouse and human phenotypes.

claim: Mice homozygous for a Foxc1hith/hith hypomorphic allele are viable as adults and have abnormal cerebellar foliation.
source: We previously reported that mice homozygous for a Foxc1hith/hithhypomorphic allele are viable as adults and have abnormal cerebellar foliation (Aldinger et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Foxc1hith/hith mice retain 5% Foxc1 activity.
source: These mice retain 5% Foxc1 activity (Zarbalis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zarbalis et al., 2007.

claim: Foxc1hith/hith mice have a highly unusual, partially formed posterior lobule (lobule X), which aberrantly exposes the internal granule layer to the fourth ventricle.
source: Here, we add to our previous report, showing that Foxc1hith/hithmice have a highly unusual, partially formed posterior lobule (lobule X), which aberrantly exposes the internal granule layer to the fourth ventricle.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1I,J.

claim: The Foxc1hith/hith posterior lobule phenotype is reminiscent of the human DWM tail.
source: This phenotype is reminiscent of the human DWM tail (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of mouse and human phenotypes shown in Figure 1.

claim: Foxc1hith/hith mice are the only mouse model to consistently show the partially formed posterior lobule foliation phenotype.
source: To our knowledge, Foxc1hith/hith mice are the only mouse model to consistently show this foliation phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as a unique feature of this model based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: Cerebellar foliation normally follows a stereotypic pattern and sequence.
source: Cerebellar foliation normally follows a stereotypic pattern and sequence.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cerebellar development.

claim: Four cardinal vermis fissures, including the primary and secondary fissures, are anchored late in embryonic mouse development.
source: Four cardinal vermis fissures, including the primary and secondary fissures, are anchored late in embryonic mouse development, then additional fissure formation and folia lengthening progress postnatally (Sudarov and Joyner, 2007; Legué et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sudarov and Joyner, 2007 and Legué et al., 2015.

claim: Additional fissure formation and folia lengthening progress postnatally in mice.
source: Four cardinal vermis fissures, including the primary and secondary fissures, are anchored late in embryonic mouse development, then additional fissure formation and folia lengthening progress postnatally (Sudarov and Joyner, 2007; Legué et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sudarov and Joyner, 2007 and Legué et al., 2015.

claim: The primary and secondary fissures were readily evident at P15 in both wild-type and Foxc1hith/hith mice.
source: Although the primary and secondary fissures were readily evident at P15 (Postnatal day 15) in both wild-type and Foxc1hith/hith mice, a delay in posterior fissure formation was evident at P1 in Foxc1hith/hith mice, (Figure 1M,N; asterisks) and the Foxc1hith/hith posterior vermis was clearly disorganized at this stage (Figure 1N).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1M,N.

claim: A delay in posterior fissure formation was evident at P1 in Foxc1hith/hith mice.
source: Although the primary and secondary fissures were readily evident at P15 (Postnatal day 15) in both wild-type and Foxc1hith/hith mice, a delay in posterior fissure formation was evident at P1 in Foxc1hith/hith mice, (Figure 1M,N; asterisks) and the Foxc1hith/hith posterior vermis was clearly disorganized at this stage (Figure 1N).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1M,N.

claim: The Foxc1hith/hith posterior vermis was clearly disorganized at P1.
source: Although the primary and secondary fissures were readily evident at P15 (Postnatal day 15) in both wild-type and Foxc1hith/hith mice, a delay in posterior fissure formation was evident at P1 in Foxc1hith/hith mice, (Figure 1M,N; asterisks) and the Foxc1hith/hith posterior vermis was clearly disorganized at this stage (Figure 1N).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1N.

claim: At e17.5, the Foxc1hith/hith RL was very disorganized with an abnormal abundance of apparent GCP.
source: At e17.5, the Foxc1hith/hith RL was very disorganized with an abnormal abundance of apparent GCP (Figure 1P) (Ki67+/Pax6+ data not shown), similar to the RL phenotype we previously reported in embryonic Foxc1-/- mice (Aldinger et al., 2009; Haldipur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1P and citations to previous work.

claim: In e17.5 WT animals, Lmx1a-cre is expressed in the subset of embryonic cerebellar RL cells fated to give rise to the fourth ventricle choroid plexus epithelium, GCPs, and their descendants which are restricted to the posterior vermis (lobule X and the posterior half of lobule IX), and unipolar brush cells within the core of the developing cerebellum.
source: In e17.5 WT animals (Figure 2A), Lmx1a-cre is expressed in the subset of embryonic cerebellar RL cells fated to give rise to the fourth ventricle choroid plexus epithelium, GCPs, and their descendants which are restricted to the posterior vermis (lobule X and the posterior half of lobule IX), and unipolar brush cells within the core of the developing cerebellum (Chizhikov et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chizhikov et al., 2010 and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: By P0, the RL had fully regressed in wild-type animals and the RL-derived Lmx1a-labeled lineages were clearly limited to lobule X and the posterior half of lobule IX.
source: As expected, by P0, the RL had fully regressed in wild-type animals and the RL-derived Lmx1a-labeled lineages were clearly limited to lobule X and the posterior half of lobule IX (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Lmx1a expression was not dependent on Foxc1 expression.
source: We next determined that Lmx1a expression was not dependent on Foxc1 expression.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At the onset of Lmx1a RL expression at e13.5, there was no difference in Lmx1a expression between WT and Foxc1-/-.
source: At the onset of Lmx1a RL expression at e13.5, there was no difference in Lmx1a expression between WT and Foxc1-/-(Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: By e17.5, in Foxc1hith/hith mice, Lmx1a-cre marked cells remained restricted to the posterior vermis yet the RL retained an excess of labeled cells.
source: By e17.5, however, in Foxc1hith/hith mice, Lmx1a-cre marked cells remained restricted to the posterior vermis yet the RL retained an excess of labeled cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Many streams of Lmx1a-lineage marked cells were aberrantly located within the core of the developing cerebellum in Foxc1hith/hith mice at e17.5.
source: Many streams of Lmx1a-lineage marked cells were also aberrantly located within the core of the developing cerebellum in addition to cells normally traversing into the External Granule Layer (EGL) (Figure 2B, arrows).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: By P0, labelled EGL cells had ectopically migrated anteriorly to the secondary fissure, the anterior boundary of lobule IX in the Foxc1hith/hith mutants.
source: By P0, labelled EGL cells had ectopically migrated anteriorly to the secondary fissure, the anterior boundary of lobule IX in the Foxc1hith/hith mutants (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Large numbers of Lmx1a-fate mapped cells were observed along a residual posterior ventricular zone in Foxc1hith/hith mutants at P0.
source: We also observed large numbers of Lmx1a-fate mapped cells along a residual posterior ventricular zone in Foxc1hith/hith mutants (Figure 2D, yellow arrow).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In wild-type embryos, most Lmx1a-cre labelled cells exited the RL and migrated into the posterior EGL between e14.5 and e17.5.
source: As expected, in wild-type embryos, most Lmx1a-cre labelled cells exited the RL and migrated into the posterior EGL between e14.5 and e17.5 (Figure 2E,G,I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E,G,I.

claim: In Foxc1-/- mutants, dramatic mismigration of the posterior-fated RL lineage was evident as early as e14.5.
source: In Foxc1-/-mutants, however, dramatic mismigration of the posterior-fated RL lineage was evident as early as e14.5 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: By e17.5 in Foxc1-/- mutants, an abnormally large RL showed numerous retained Lmx1a-cre+ cells.
source: By e17.5, an abnormally large RL showed numerous retained Lmx1a-cre+ cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Ectopic Lmx1a-cre+ streams of cells were present along the VZ in Foxc1-/- mutants at e17.5.
source: Ectopic Lmx1a-cre+ streams of cells were also present along the VZ (Figure 2H,J).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2H,J.

claim: There are significantly higher numbers of ectopic tdTomato+ cells in Foxc1-/- mutants compared to wild-type.
source: Quantification of tdTomato+ cells present outside of the EGL and RL area in the wild-type and Foxc1-/-mutants indicates significantly higher numbers of ectopic tdTomato+ cells in the mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RL and VZ development in Foxc1-/- mutants is more severely disrupted than in Foxc1hith/hith.
source: Thus, RL and VZ development in Foxc1-/- mutants is more severely disrupted than in Foxc1hith/hith (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) (Haldipur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing data between the two mutant models.

claim: Lmx1a-lineage marked (tdTomato+) cells in the e17.5 Foxc1-/- cerebellar anlage core did not include VZ progenitors (Sox9+), GABAergic interneurons (Pax2+) or Purkinje cells (Skor2+).
source: We tested if Lmx1a-fate mapped cells found in the e17.5 Foxc1-/-cerebellar anlage core were incorrectly derived from re-specified VZ fates. We did not however detect any Lmx1a-lineage marked (tdTomato+) VZ progenitors (Sox9+), GABAergic interneurons (Pax2+) or Purkinje cells (Skor2+) (Figure 2K–M).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2K–M.

claim: All tdTomato+ cells in the e17.5 Foxc1-/- cerebellar anlage retained a Pax6+ RL lineage identity.
source: Rather, all tdTomato+ cells retained a Pax6+ RL lineage identity (Figure 2O–P, arrows).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2O–P.

claim: A subset of the internally-located tdTomato+ Lmx1a-fate mapped cells was Tbr2+ positive, consistent with the unipolar brush cell fate expected from the RL Lmx1a+ lineage.
source: As expected, a subset of the internally-located tdTomato+ Lmx1a-fate mapped cells was Tbr2+ positive (Figure 2N,n, arrows), consistent with the unipolar brush cell fate expected from the RL Lmx1a+ lineage.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2N,n.

claim: A large subset of the misrouted GCPs continues to proliferate in Foxc1-/- mutants.
source: However, we note that while a large subset of the misrouted GCPs continues to proliferate (Figure 2Q, red and yellow arrow; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D, arrows), we also observe that many of the Lmx1a-cre tdTomato+ cells that fail to migrate out of the RL eventually differentiate precociously within the RL (Figure 2R).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2Q and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Many of the Lmx1a-cre tdTomato+ cells that fail to migrate out of the RL eventually differentiate precociously within the RL in Foxc1-/- mutants.
source: However, we note that while a large subset of the misrouted GCPs continues to proliferate (Figure 2Q, red and yellow arrow; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D, arrows), we also observe that many of the Lmx1a-cre tdTomato+ cells that fail to migrate out of the RL eventually differentiate precociously within the RL (Figure 2R).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2R.

claim: A combination of mismigration and precocious differentiation causes a depletion of granule cell progenitors required to form the posterior vermis, leading to severely hypoplastic posterior lobules in Foxc1hith/hith mice.
source: We conclude that a combination of mismigration and precocious differentiation causes a depletion of granule cell progenitors required to form the posterior vermis, thus leading to severely hypoplastic posterior lobules in Foxc1hith/hith mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the data presented.

claim: In wild-type animals, proliferating GCPs were restricted to the outer EGL at e19.5.
source: In wild-type animals, proliferating GCPs were restricted to the outer EGL (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, inset).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In Foxc1-/- embryos at e19.5, streams of proliferating GCPs from the EGL ectopically migrated into the cerebellar core.
source: However, in Foxc1-/- embryos, we consistently observed streams of proliferating GCPs from the EGL ectopically migrating into the cerebellar core.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–D.

claim: Some streams of ectopic GCPs disrupted the nascent Purkinje cell plate under the EGL in Foxc1-/- embryos at e19.5.
source: Some of these streams disrupted the nascent Purkinje cell plate under the EGL, further contributing to the profound disorganization of the Foxc1-/- mutant cerebellum (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–D, arrows).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–D.

claim: GCPs secrete reelin as a chemoattractant to Purkinje cells radially migrating outward from their VZ origin.
source: Since GCPs secrete reelin as a chemoattractant to Purkinje cells radially migrating outward from their VZ origin, it was not surprising to observe ectopic Purkinje cells within the core of the developing cerebellum together with ectopic granule cells in Foxc1-/- mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F,H, boxes).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cerebellar development.

claim: Ectopic Purkinje cells were observed within the core of the developing cerebellum together with ectopic granule cells in Foxc1-/- mutants at e19.5.
source: Since GCPs secrete reelin as a chemoattractant to Purkinje cells radially migrating outward from their VZ origin, it was not surprising to observe ectopic Purkinje cells within the core of the developing cerebellum together with ectopic granule cells in Foxc1-/- mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F,H, boxes).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F,H.

claim: At least some of the centrally-located ectopic Purkinje cells in Foxc1-/- mutants were the result of aborted outward radial migration of Purkinje cells out of the VZ due to the disruption of the radial scaffold.
source: We also expect that at least some of these centrally-located ectopic Purkinje cells were the result of aborted outward radial migration of Purkinje cells out of the VZ due to the disruption of the radial scaffold in Foxc1-/- mutants, a phenotype that we previously reported (Haldipur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from previous findings and current observations.

claim: In wild-type animals, the maturing Purkinje cells organize into a monolayer evident around P16.
source: In wild-type animals, the maturing Purkinje cells organize into a monolayer evident around P16 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2I), while in Foxc1hith/hith mice, we observed multilayered Purkinje cells in addition to ectopic Purkinje cells fully embedded within the internal granule cell layer (IGL) in multiple lobules (Figure 2—figure supplement 2J–L, arrows, box).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2I.

claim: In Foxc1hith/hith mice at P16, multilayered Purkinje cells were observed in addition to ectopic Purkinje cells fully embedded within the internal granule cell layer (IGL) in multiple lobules.
source: In wild-type animals, the maturing Purkinje cells organize into a monolayer evident around P16 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2I), while in Foxc1hith/hith mice, we observed multilayered Purkinje cells in addition to ectopic Purkinje cells fully embedded within the internal granule cell layer (IGL) in multiple lobules (Figure 2—figure supplement 2J–L, arrows, box).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2J–L.

claim: Foliation and lamination abnormalities observed in postnatal Foxc1hith/hith mouse mutants are reminiscent of defects observed following meningeal cell destruction by chemical treatment with 6-OHDA in neonatal hamsters.
source: Both foliation and lamination abnormalities observed in postnatal Foxc1hith/hith mouse mutants are reminiscent of defects observed following meningeal cell destruction by chemical treatment with 6-OHDA in neonatal hamsters (von Knebel Doeberitz et al., 1986), which caused disorganized radially oriented glial fibers due to loss of contact with absent meninges.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work cited (von Knebel Doeberitz et al., 1986).

claim: In postnatal Foxc1hith/hith cerebella, GFAP immunostaining for Bergmann glial fibers showed normal radial fiber organization.
source: However, in postnatal Foxc1hith/hith cerebella, GFAP immunostaining for Bergmann glial fibers showed normal radial fiber organization (Figure 2—figure supplement 2N).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2N.

claim: Laminin immunostaining, which highlights the pial basement membrane, was neither different from wild-type nor discontinuous in early postnatal Foxc1hith/hith cerebella.
source: Laminin immunostaining, which highlights the pial basement membrane, was neither different from wild-type nor discontinuous in early postnatal Foxc1hith/hith cerebella (Figure 2—figure supplement 2P).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2P.

claim: The Foxc1hith/hith phenotype is consistent with a loss of Foxc1-dependent SDF1α signaling.
source: Rather, the Foxc1hith/hith phenotype is consistent with a loss of Foxc1-dependent SDF1α signaling (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), which we have previously shown to be responsible for a number of embryonic phenotypes, in particular, the loss of radial glial structure and aberrations in cell migration of both the VZ and RL in Foxc1-/- mice (Haldipur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and previous work cited.

claim: Loss of Foxc1-dependent SDF1α signaling is responsible for the loss of radial glial structure and aberrations in cell migration of both the VZ and RL in Foxc1-/- mice.
source: Rather, the Foxc1hith/hith phenotype is consistent with a loss of Foxc1-dependent SDF1α signaling (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), which we have previously shown to be responsible for a number of embryonic phenotypes, in particular, the loss of radial glial structure and aberrations in cell migration of both the VZ and RL in Foxc1-/- mice (Haldipur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Haldipur et al., 2014).

claim: A recent study by Delahaye et al. (2012) identified three human fetal del chr 6p25 DWM cases with large deletions (6.6–17 Mb) encompassing the FOXC1 gene.
source: Importantly, a recent study by Delahaye et al. (2012) identified three human fetal del chr 6p25 DWM cases with large deletions (6.6–17 Mb) encompassing the FOXC1 gene.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Delahaye et al. (2012).

claim: No posterior fossa anomalies were detected either by prenatal ultrasound or autopsy in control fetal cases.
source: No posterior fossa anomalies were detected either by prenatal ultrasound or autopsy in these control cases.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the control cases used in the study.

claim: In control fetal cases, all histogenic layers of the developing cerebellum appeared normal.
source: Low magnification images of the H and E stained cerebellar vermis from the control cases indicated normal development of the folia. All histogenic layers of the developing cerebellum appeared normal.
evidence: This is supported by observations from Figure 3A–C.

claim: In control fetal cases, the EGL was of uniform thickness across the cerebella.
source: The EGL was of uniform thickness across the cerebella and the Purkinje cells formed a continuous multilayer Purkinje cell plate under the EGL from the anterior to posterior lobes (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: In control fetal cases, the Purkinje cells formed a continuous multilayer Purkinje cell plate under the EGL from the anterior to posterior lobes.
source: The EGL was of uniform thickness across the cerebella and the Purkinje cells formed a continuous multilayer Purkinje cell plate under the EGL from the anterior to posterior lobes (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: In all del chr 6p25 fetal cases, striking foliation defects of varying severity were observed.
source: In all del chr 6p25 cases, striking foliation defects of varying severity were observed (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D–F.

claim: In the cerebellum with the least severe DWM phenotype, DW1, the posterior-most lobule, lobule X, was only partially formed.
source: In the cerebellum with the least severe DWM phenotype, DW1, the posterior-most lobule, lobule X, was only partially formed (Figure 3D,G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D,G.

claim: In DW1, the anterior lobules appeared relatively normal.
source: However, the anterior lobules appeared relatively normal.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3D.

claim: The defects in cerebellar foliation were far more severe in del chr 6p25 cases DW2 and DW3.
source: The defects in cerebellar foliation were far more severe in the other two del chr 6p25 cases, DW2 and DW3.
evidence: This is supported by observations from Figure 3E,F.

claim: In DW2 and DW3, the vermis was hypoplastic with the most severe hypoplasia and dysplasia readily evident in the posterior vermis.
source: In both cases, the vermis was hypoplastic with the most severe hypoplasia and dysplasia readily evident in the posterior vermis, despite obvious artefactual tissue damage.
evidence: This is supported by observations from Figure 3E,F.

claim: In DW2 and DW3, even the lobules in the anterior vermis were not readily distinguishable, with rudimentary fissures defining several lobules of variably indistinct identity.
source: Yet, even the lobules in the anterior vermis were not readily distinguishable, with rudimentary fissures defining several lobules of variably indistinct identity. (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is supported by observations from Figure 3E,F.

claim: Although the posterior-most vermis was missing in DW3, the remaining posterior surface of DW3 was remarkably flat with no recognizable fissures.
source: Although the posterior-most vermis was missing in DW3, the remaining posterior surface of DW3 was remarkably flat with no recognizable fissures (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by observations from Figure 3F.

claim: Heterotopic cell clusters were evident with H and E staining in all of the DW cases.
source: Unique to all of the DW cases, heterotopic cell clusters were evident with H and E staining. These were particularly prominent in DW1 (Figure 3D,G–I).
evidence: This is supported by observations from Figure 3D,G–I.

claim: In DW1, at the base of the fissure between lobules IV and V, an ectopic calbindin+ Purkinje cell cluster was evident.
source: For example, at the base of the fissure between lobules IV and V, an ectopic calbindin+ Purkinje cell cluster was evident.
evidence: This is supported by observations from Figure 3H,I.

claim: In DW1, just above the ectopic Purkinje cell cluster, numerous proliferating Ki67+ Pax6+ GCPs were apparent.
source: Just above this, numerous proliferating Ki67+ Pax6+ GCPs were also apparent.
evidence: This is supported by observations from Figure 3J–L.

claim: Similar ectopic clusters of Purkinje cells and GCPs were observed in DW2 and DW3.
source: Similar ectopic clusters of Purkinje cells and GCPs were also observed in the other two DW cases (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation, though data is not shown.

claim: In control fetal cases, the Purkinje cell layer was well-defined, consisting of a distinct multilayer band of cells beneath the molecular layer, above the internal granule layer.
source: In the control cases, the Purkinje cell layer was well-defined, consisting of a distinct multilayer band of cells beneath the molecular layer, above the internal granule layer (Figure 4A–C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: In all three del chr 6p25 cases, Purkinje cells were located in a highly disorganized diffuse layer beneath the EGL.
source: In all three del chr 6p25 cases, Purkinje cells were located in a highly disorganized diffuse layer beneath the EGL.
evidence: This is supported by observations from Figure 4G–I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: Purkinje cell disorganization was most marked in the posterior vermis in del chr 6p25 cases.
source: This was most marked in the posterior vermis, although in the more severe cases (DW2 and DW3), Purkinje cells were disorganized anteriorly as well (Figure 4G–I; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by observations from Figure 4G–I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: In all 3 DW cases, Purkinje cells lacked their characteristic dendritic arborization, indicating at least a delay in Purkinje cell development.
source: Higher magnification of calbindin-stained sections revealed that in all 3 DW cases, Purkinje cells also lacked their characteristic dendritic arborization, indicating at least a delay in Purkinje cell development.
evidence: This is inferred from observations in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ectopic Purkinje cells were found in the Internal Granule Layer (IGL) and cerebellar white matter in del chr 6p25 cases.
source: Ectopic Purkinje cells were also found in the Internal Granule Layer (IGL) and cerebellar white matter (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: All human control samples, regardless of age, had well defined GFAP+ Bergmann glial fibers extending from the EGL to the Purkinje cell layer where their bodies reside.
source: As expected, all human control samples, regardless of age, had well defined GFAP+ Bergmann glial fibers extending from the EGL to the Purkinje cell layer where their bodies reside (Figure 4G–I; Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4G–I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: Bergmann glial fiber morphology was normal in Foxc1hith/hith mouse mutants.
source: While Bergmann glial fiber morphology was normal in Foxc1hith/hith mouse mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2M,N), their morphology, number, and location were affected in the Foxc1-/- cerebellum (Haldipur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2M,N.

claim: Bergmann glial fiber morphology, number, and location were affected in the Foxc1-/- cerebellum.
source: While Bergmann glial fiber morphology was normal in Foxc1hith/hith mouse mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2M,N), their morphology, number, and location were affected in the Foxc1-/- cerebellum (Haldipur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Haldipur et al., 2014).

claim: In all three fetal del chr 6p25 cases, fewer Bergmann glial fibers were evident, with some regions devoid of Bergmann glia fibers entirely.
source: Consistent with Foxc1-/- mouse data, in all three fetal del chr 6p25 cases, fewer Bergmann glial fibers were evident, with some regions devoid of Bergmann glia fibers entirely (Figure 4J–L; Figure 4—figure supplement 1J–L).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4J–L and Figure 4—figure supplement 1J–L.

claim: Remaining Bergmann glial fibers were severely dysmorphic in all three fetal del chr 6p25 cases.
source: Remaining Bergmann glial fibers were severely dysmorphic.
evidence: This is supported by observations from Figure 4J–L and Figure 4—figure supplement 1J–L.

claim: The Bergmann glial fiber deficits in del chr 6p25 cases may be related to the direct requirement of SDF1α to maintain cerebellar Bergmann glial fibers.
source: This may be related to the direct requirement of SDF1α to maintain cerebellar Bergmann glial fibers (Haldipur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from previous work cited (Haldipur et al., 2014).

claim: Purkinje cell deficits may contribute to Bergmann glial fiber abnormalities, since radial glial maintenance also depends on normal Purkinje cell development.
source: Purkinje cell deficits may also contribute to this phenotype, since radial glial maintenance also depends on normal Purkinje cell development (Dahmane and Ruiz i Altaba, 1999).
evidence: This is inferred from previous work cited (Dahmane and Ruiz i Altaba, 1999).

claim: The striking similarities in phenotype between Foxc1 mouse mutant cerebella and the human del chr 6p25 DWM cases validate the mouse Foxc1 mutant mouse models.
source: The striking similarities in phenotype between Foxc1 mouse mutant cerebella and the human del chr 6p25 DWM cases validate our mouse Foxc1 mutant mouse models and suggest that many of the key mechanisms controlling cerebellar development are conserved between mouse and human.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative analyses presented.

claim: The diagnosis of DWM has improved with advances in brain imaging.
source: Although the diagnosis of DWM has improved with advances in brain imaging (Doherty et al., 2013), the mechanisms leading to this important human cerebellar malformation remain largely unknown.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Doherty et al., 2013.

claim: The mechanisms leading to DWM remain largely unknown.
source: Although the diagnosis of DWM has improved with advances in brain imaging (Doherty et al., 2013), the mechanisms leading to this important human cerebellar malformation remain largely unknown.
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge in the field.

claim: A few genes have been implicated in rare cases of DWM.
source: A few genes have been implicated in rare cases of DWM (Aldinger and Doherty, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Aldinger and Doherty, 2016.

claim: Of genes implicated in DWM, FOXC1 is the best studied.
source: Of these, FOXC1 is the best studied (Aldinger et al., 2009; Haldipur et al., 2014), with mutant mouse data demonstrating several important roles for Foxc1 in early mouse cerebellar anlage development.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Foxc1 expression is largely limited to the posterior fossa mesenchyme rather than the developing cerebellum itself.
source: Notably, Foxc1 expression is largely limited to the posterior fossa mesenchyme rather than the developing cerebellum itself.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about Foxc1 expression.

claim: Complete loss of Foxc1 in mice leads to loss of Foxc1-dependent expression of SDF1α, a secreted factor in the posterior mesenchyme.
source: Complete loss of Foxc1 in mice (homozygous null animals) leads to loss of Foxc1-dependent expression of SDF1α, a secreted factor in the posterior mesenchyme.
evidence: This is stated as a known finding from previous work.

claim: SDF1α acts via its receptor, Cxcr4, which is expressed in cerebellar radial glial cells.
source: We previously showed that SDF1α acts via its receptor, Cxcr4, which is expressed in cerebellar radial glial cells and is required for both proliferation of these VZ progenitors in addition to maintenance of their radial fibers, which are the migration scaffold for cerebellar GABAergic neurons to reach the cerebellar cortex (Haldipur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Haldipur et al., 2014).

claim: SDF1α is required for both proliferation of VZ progenitors and maintenance of their radial fibers, which are the migration scaffold for cerebellar GABAergic neurons to reach the cerebellar cortex.
source: We previously showed that SDF1α acts via its receptor, Cxcr4, which is expressed in cerebellar radial glial cells and is required for both proliferation of these VZ progenitors in addition to maintenance of their radial fibers, which are the migration scaffold for cerebellar GABAergic neurons to reach the cerebellar cortex (Haldipur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Haldipur et al., 2014).

claim: The Foxc1-/- phenotype is much more severe than that seen in human DWM patients (del chr 6p25), who harbor a deletion of the FOXC1 gene, yet retain one intact copy on an unaffected chromosome.
source: Notably, the Foxc1-/- phenotype is much more severe than that seen in human DWM patients (del chr 6p25), who harbor a deletion of the FOXC1 gene, yet retain one intact copy on an unaffected chromosome (Aldinger et al., 2009; Delahaye et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing mouse and human phenotypes, supported by citations.

claim: Foxc1+/- mice have no cerebellar phenotype.
source: Foxc1+/- mice have no cerebellar phenotype, however, Foxc1hith/hith are postnatal viable and have disrupted cerebellar morphology (Aldinger et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Aldinger et al., 2009).

claim: Foxc1hith/hith mice display a unique posterior vermis foliation defect that is strikingly similar to that shared with all human del chr 6p25 DWM patients.
source: We have now shown that Foxc1hith/hith mutants display a unique posterior vermis foliation defect that is strikingly similar to that shared with all human del chr 6p25 DWM patients.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Using lineage fate mapping in mouse models, embryonic migration abnormalities of the posterior-fated cerebellar RL descendants causes the posterior vermis phenotype in both Foxc1hith/hith and Foxc1-/- mice.
source: Using lineage fate mapping in mouse models, we demonstrated that embryonic migration abnormalities of the posterior-fated cerebellar RL descendants causes this phenotype in both Foxc1hith/hith and Foxc1-/- mice and showed that Foxc1hith/hith mice also display defects in postnatal cerebellar lamination.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by lineage mapping data.

claim: Foxc1hith/hith mice display defects in postnatal cerebellar lamination.
source: Using lineage fate mapping in mouse models, we demonstrated that embryonic migration abnormalities of the posterior-fated cerebellar RL descendants causes this phenotype in both Foxc1hith/hith and Foxc1-/- mice and showed that Foxc1hith/hith mice also display defects in postnatal cerebellar lamination.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: This report represents the first in-depth analysis of human fetal DWM.
source: To our knowledge, this report represents the first in-depth analysis of human fetal DWM.
evidence: This is stated as a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: All three human del chr 6p25 fetal DWM fetal cases exhibited a striking dysplasia of the posterior vermis.
source: All three human del chr 6p25 fetal DWM fetal cases we assessed here exhibited a striking dysplasia of the posterior vermis and also had ectopically located GCPs and Purkinje cells and dysmorphic and sparse Bergmann glial fibers.
evidence: This is supported by observations from Figures 3 and 4.

claim: All three human del chr 6p25 fetal DWM cases had ectopically located GCPs and Purkinje cells and dysmorphic and sparse Bergmann glial fibers.
source: All three human del chr 6p25 fetal DWM fetal cases we assessed here exhibited a striking dysplasia of the posterior vermis and also had ectopically located GCPs and Purkinje cells and dysmorphic and sparse Bergmann glial fibers.
evidence: This is supported by observations from Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The phenotypes observed in the del chr 6p25 cerebella are similar to those observed in the Foxc1-/- mouse.
source: The phenotypes observed in the del chr 6p25 cerebella are similar to those observed in the Foxc1-/- mouse, providing ample evidence of the validity of our Foxc1-/- DWM models.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative analyses presented.

claim: Human fetal DWM cases are snapshots of three separate dysmorphic cerebella at specific stages of development (18–21 gw).
source: The human fetal DWM cases presented here are snapshots of three separate dysmorphic cerebella at specific stages of development (18–21 gw).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: A thorough study of multiple stages of abnormal prenatal cerebellar development will be nearly impossible given the clinical constraints of human fetal tissue research and the rarity of genetically defined malformation cases.
source: Given the clinical constraints of human fetal tissue research and the rarity of genetically defined malformation cases, a thorough study of multiple stages of abnormal prenatal cerebellar development will be nearly impossible.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation and challenge in the field.

claim: DWM is not currently readily diagnosed by imaging until 18 gw.
source: Further, since DWM is not currently readily diagnosed by imaging until 18 gw, it is likely impossible to obtain earlier cases.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation in the field.

claim: Human fetal analysis is essential because it is the only analysis that is possible for studying human DWM development.
source: However, human fetal analysis, as we have presented here, is essential because it is the only analysis that is possible.
evidence: This is stated as justification for the study approach.

claim: Animal models are required to investigate potential mechanisms of DWM.
source: Animal models are required to investigate potential mechanisms and our current work clearly validates our Foxc1 mutant mouse models.
evidence: This is stated as justification for using mouse models.

claim: Mouse models indicate that human del chr 6p25 DWM is largely due to a disruption of early mesenchymal signaling and aberrant rhombic lip development.
source: Since our mouse models indicate that human del chr 6p25 DWM is largely due to a disruption of early mesenchymal signaling and aberrant rhombic lip development, a long term goal is to develop human fetal imaging technology and protocols targeted to these phenotypes to facilitate earlier detection and perhaps provide therapeutic intervention.
evidence: This is inferred from the data presented in the study.

claim: Early disruption in mesenchymal signaling has immediate effects, including mismigration of Purkinje cells and GCPs from both the RL and EGL.
source: In conclusion, this study presents an analysis of the changes that take place during mouse and human cerebellar development following the loss of Foxc1 and subsequent disruptions in mesenchymal signaling. We show that early disruption in mesenchymal signaling has immediate effects, including mismigration of Purkinje cells and GCPs from both the RL and EGL.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study supported by the data presented.

claim: There are both direct and indirect repercussions on later developmental events that lead to abnormal foliation, posterior vermis hypoplasia, developmental delays, and abnormal layering of Purkinje cells following loss of Foxc1.
source: There are both direct and indirect repercussions on later developmental events that lead to abnormal foliation, posterior vermis hypoplasia, developmental delays, and abnormal layering of Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study supported by the data presented.

claim: Human and mouse analyses provide compelling evidence to support the model of Foxc1 control of cerebellar development and developmental pathogenesis of FOXC1-dependent DWM.
source: Together our human and mouse analyses provide compelling evidence to support our model of Foxc1 control of cerebellar development and developmental pathogenesis of FOXC1-dependent DWM (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study supported by the data presented and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: An essential question remains as to whether the key features and mechanisms elucidated for Foxc1-dependent DWM are generalizable to all forms of DWM, regardless of the underlying genotype.
source: Notably, however, human del chr 6p25 DWM cases are rare. An essential question remains as to whether the key features and mechanisms we have elucidated for Foxc1-dependent DWM are generalizable to all forms of DWM, regardless of the underlying genotype.
evidence: This is stated as an open question for future research.

claim: SDF1α expressed in the head mesenchyme is a direct transcriptional target of Foxc1.
source: SDF1α expressed in the head mesenchyme is a direct transcriptional target of Foxc1 (Zarbalis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zarbalis et al., 2012.

claim: Loss of SDF1α can rescue Foxc1-/- cerebellar phenotypes.
source: We have demonstrated that loss of SDF1α can rescue Foxc1-/- cerebellar phenotypes (Haldipur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Haldipur et al., 2014).

claim: At e12.5, when Foxc1 expression is initiated in the posterior fossa mesenchyme overlying the cerebellum, SDF1α expression is significantly downregulated in both Foxc1-/- and Foxc1hith/hith embryos.
source: At e12.5, when Foxc1 expression is initiated in the posterior fossa mesenchyme overlying the cerebellum, SDF1α expression is significantly downregulated in both Foxc1-/- and Foxc1hith/hith embryos at e12.5 (Aldinger et al., 2009) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and a citation to previous work.

claim: Foxc1 is required to maintain, but not initiate, SDF1α expression.
source: Since SDF1α is expressed in the mouse posterior fossa mesenchyme prior to e12.5 ([Lein et al., 2007], Website: © 2015 Allen Institute for Brain Science. Allen Mouse Brain Atlas [Internet]. Available from: http://mouse.brain-map.org.), we conclude that Foxc1 is required to maintain, but not initiate, SDF1α.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of Foxc1 and SDF1α expression, supported by a citation.

claim: The maintenance role of Foxc1 for SDF1α is key to understanding the increased vulnerability of the posterior vermis in Foxc1 mouse mutants and human del chr 6p25 DWM.
source: This maintenance role is key to understanding the increased vulnerability of the posterior vermis in Foxc1 mouse mutants and human del chr 6p25 DWM.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and discussion presented.

claim: SDF1α secreted by embryonic meningeal cells embryonically acts as a chemoattractant, regulating the tangential migration of Cxcr4+ GCPs away from the RL to form the EGL.
source: Previous studies have shown that SDF1α secreted by embryonic meningeal cells embryonically acts as a chemoattractant, regulating the tangential migration of Cxcr4+ GCPs away from the RL to form the EGL (Yu et al., 2010; Haldipur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Yu et al., 2010; Haldipur et al., 2014).

claim: The cerebellar RL generates assorted glutamatergic brain stem nuclei and cerebellar nuclei in the mouse at e10.5 and anteriorly fated GCPs just before e12.5.
source: The cerebellar RL generates assorted glutamatergic brain stem nuclei and cerebellar nuclei in the mouse at e10.5 and anteriorly fated GCPs just before e12.5 (Machold and Fishell, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Machold and Fishell, 2005.

claim: By e12.5, only posterior vermis-fated GCPs and unipolar brush cells remain in the RL to emerge over the remaining days of mouse embryogenesis.
source: By e12.5, only posterior vermis-fated GCPs and unipolar brush cells remain in the RL to emerge over the remaining days of mouse embryogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cerebellar development.

claim: Late RL derivatives are absolutely dependent on continued SDF1α expression which itself is dependent on Foxc1.
source: Our new data clearly demonstrates that these late derivatives are absolutely dependent on continued SDF1α expression which itself is dependent on Foxc1.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study supported by the data presented.

claim: SDF1α acts as a chemoattractant in the developing pia to maintain GCPs within the proliferating outer zone of the developing EGL adjacent to the pial surface.
source: Our data also confirm previous studies showing a role for SDF1α as a chemoattractant in the developing pia to maintain GCPs within the proliferating outer zone of the developing EGL adjacent to the pial surface (Hartmann et al., 1998; Wiegand et al., 1998; Zou et al., 1998; Reiss et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2002; Vilz et al., 2005; Tiveron and Cremer, 2008; Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: In Foxc1 mutants, SDF1α is not maintained at appropriate levels, leading to ectopic proliferating EGL cells within the cerebellar anlage in both the anterior and posterior vermis.
source: In Foxc1 mutants, SDF1α is not maintained at appropriate levels, leading to an additional phenotype of ectopic proliferating EGL cells within the cerebellar anlage in both the anterior and posterior vermis.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study supported by the data presented.

claim: The posterior fossa mesenchyme, through SDF1α expression, preserves the structure of both the RL and the nascent EGL.
source: Our results add to the growing body of evidence that the posterior fossa mesenchyme, through SDF1α expression, preserves the structure of both the RL and the nascent EGL.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study supported by the data presented.

claim: By ensuring that cells correctly exit the RL and remain within the GCP niche of the EGL, the mesenchyme regulates the proper formation and lamination of cerebellar folia.
source: By ensuring that cells correctly exit the RL and remain within the GCP niche of the EGL, the mesenchyme regulates the proper formation and lamination of cerebellar folia (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study supported by the data presented and illustrated in Figure 5.
